summary: Specifies Virtual Enterprise Traversal, a way to automatically provision addresses and prefixes and support internetworking across the varied link types of enterprise networks, including those connected to provider networks or the Internet. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Companies link many kinds of networks together. This note describes a method that sets up addresses and connections by itself so administrators have less to do.

questions: how are ip prefixes provisioned across enterprise networks automatically
how does vet present an enterprise as a single ip hop
what is the difference between rlocs and eids
how are enterprise border routers discovered in vet
subtitle: Automatic provisioning and routing for enterprise networks of varied link types.

tldr.problem: Enterprise networks connect routers over different link types, including wireless, Ethernet, tunnels, and connections to provider networks. Enterprises need a way to automatically assign IP addresses and prefixes to nodes across this diverse environment while supporting mobility, multihoming, and various network scenarios from small offices to large corporations.
tldr.mechanism: Virtual Enterprise Traversal (VET) uses IP-in-IP encapsulation to create an overlay that presents an entire enterprise as a single IP hop, with a unified virtual link. Nodes autoconfigure addresses by requesting prefixes via DHCP or self-generating them. Enterprise routers use routing locators (RLOCs) for internal routing and endpoint identifiers (EIDs) for end-to-end communications.
tldr.outcome: VET provides autoconfiguration and internetworking operations that reduce manual administration. It handles provider-independent and provider-aggregated IP prefixes, supports both IPv4 and IPv6, and enables enterprises to function across diverse link types without per-link-type configuration logic.

facts.label: Minimum enterprise size
facts.value: A collection of routers and edge networks

facts.label: Address split mechanism
facts.value: Routing Locators (RLOCs) for routing, Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs) for communications

today: RFC 5558 is Informational. VET principles have influenced subsequent work on locator-identifier separation and enterprise network design. It has not been obsoleted, though related IETF work in the AUTOCONF, DHC, and MANET working groups continues to address similar problems.

sections.title: Enterprise Networks and the VET Abstraction
sections.content:
Enterprise networks range from small office/home office (SOHO) networks to multi-organizational corporations to the global Internet itself. They connect routers over diverse link types and may also connect to provider networks. Mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) are a challenging example where topology changes dynamically.

Virtual Enterprise Traversal (VET) is an abstraction that uses IP-in-IP encapsulation to create an overlay spanning an enterprise. The overlay presents all nodes as single-hop neighbors on a virtual link, regardless of how many physical hops or different link types are traversed internally. This allows higher-layer protocols to treat the enterprise as a unified network while the overlay handles the complexity of diverse underlying links.

VET builds on IP-in-IP encapsulation principles and allows for additional encapsulations such as IPsec and SEAL (Subnetwork Encapsulation and Adaptation Layer) between inner and outer IP layers. It represents a functional superset of earlier tunnel-based approaches like 6over4 and ISATAP.
sections.plainLanguage: VET wraps data packets inside additional IP headers so they can travel across an entire enterprise network as if the whole network were a single cable connection. This hides the complexity of different network types from applications.

sections.title: Enterprise Architecture and Node Roles
sections.content:
A VET enterprise consists of routers (called Enterprise Routers or ERs) connected by links. Enterprise Border Routers (EBRs) connect edge networks to the enterprise or join multiple enterprises. Enterprise Border Gateways (EBGs) are EBRs that connect to provider networks or the Internet.

An ER has four types of interfaces: enterprise-interior interfaces connect to other routers within the enterprise; enterprise-edge interfaces connect to edge networks or hosts; provider-edge interfaces connect to external provider networks; and VET interfaces are virtual tunnel interfaces that present the enterprise as a single hop.

Each ER comprises a host function (for sending and receiving packets) and a router function (for forwarding packets). This dual role simplifies the architecture because enterprise nodes need to participate in both roles.
sections.plainLanguage: Enterprise networks have different kinds of routers: ones that stay inside the enterprise, ones that connect to the edge networks, and ones that connect to the outside world. Each type handles different jobs.

sections.title: Address Provisioning and Locator/Identifier Split
sections.content:
VET separates address provisioning into two concepts. Routing Locators (RLOCs) are IP addresses used for routing within the enterprise and at the border. They appear in routing tables and are used by routers for next-hop forwarding. RLOCs can be provider-aggregated (PA) prefixes delegated by a provider or provider-independent (PI) prefixes self-generated or allocated to the enterprise.

Endpoint Interface identifiers (EIDs) are IP addresses used by end systems and edge networks for actual communications. EIDs are typically separate from RLOCs and routable within the enterprise-edge or VET overlay scope, as well as in enterprise-interior and interdomain routing tables.

Routers autoconfigure RLOCs on enterprise-interior interfaces by requesting prefix delegations via DHCP, self-generating from private address ranges (IPv6 Unique Local Addresses or RFC 1918 IPv4 addresses), or explicit management. Edge networks receive EID prefixes, which may be PA or PI. This split allows enterprises to separate internal routing infrastructure from endpoint addressing and enables mobility and multihoming by remapping EIDs to different RLOCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The enterprise uses two kinds of addresses: inner addresses that end systems use to talk to each other, and outer addresses that routers use to forward packets across the enterprise. This separation lets enterprises change routing without breaking applications.

sections.title: Autoconfiguration Procedures
sections.content:
When an ER joins an enterprise, it first configures link-local addresses on each enterprise-interior interface for neighbor discovery. It then configures RLOCs and engages in the enterprise routing protocol.

When an EBR configures a VET interface, it initializes the interface with link-local addresses and discovers Enterprise Border Gateways. The EBR can discover EBGs through the routing protocol, through Potential Router List (PRL) discovery (resolving a DNS name like 'isatap.example.com'), through DHCP options, or through listening to multicast advertisements. Each VET interface represents a distinct enterprise connection; an EBR connecting to multiple enterprises configures one VET interface per enterprise.

EID prefixes are autoconfigured through IPv6 Router Advertisements or DHCPv6 on enterprise-edge interfaces, or through DHCPv4 for IPv4. This allows hosts and edge networks to automatically receive their end-to-end addresses without manual configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router first connects, it sets up its internal network address, finds the border gateways, and gets a block of addresses to give to the edge networks.

sections.title: Internetworking Operation and Encapsulation
sections.content:
Once configured, VET nodes participate in enterprise-interior routing using RLOCs. For communications between endpoints within the same enterprise, inner IP packets (with EID source and destination addresses) are encapsulated in outer IP headers (with RLOC source and destination addresses) and sent over enterprise-interior links. The encapsulation may include intermediate security or adaptation layers (IPsec, SEAL).

Packets traverse enterprise-interior interfaces while the TTL/Hop Limit in the inner header remains unchanged, presenting the enterprise as a single hop from the perspective of higher layers. VET interfaces in multicast-capable networks are multicast-capable; in non-multicast environments they operate as Non-Broadcast, Multiple Access (NBMA) networks.

VET also handles packet forwarding errors, mobility when nodes change attachment points, multihoming when nodes connect via multiple routers, and multicast distribution within and across enterprises. Prefix state recovery mechanisms ensure consistency when Enterprise Border Gateways change, and enterprise partitioning is handled through careful RLOC and EID management.
sections.plainLanguage: When sending data across the enterprise, the router wraps the original packet (inner) with new addressing information (outer) so it can be routed through the enterprise as a single hop.

sections.title: Security and Trust Models
sections.content:
VET requires an enterprise trust basis to be established and consistently applied. In enterprises where Enterprise Border Routers can establish symmetric security associations (such as corporate networks with centralized management), mechanisms like IPsec can be used to provide authentication and confidentiality for VET encapsulation. In enterprises with less centralized control, such as MANETs, asymmetric securing mechanisms like SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) may authenticate exchanges based on trust anchors.

The document notes that duplicate address detection (DAD) must be carefully considered in VET environments because the VET overlay may hide address collisions that would occur in the underlying networks. Nodes must reliably detect when two entities are using the same address within the enterprise.
sections.plainLanguage: Enterprises need to decide how to trust each other's routers. They can use strong encryption if all routers work together, or cryptographic signatures if the network is less organized.
